titleText.es: Neal Stephenson piensa que es bonito llamar
titleText.en: Neal Stephenson thinks it is cute to call
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive publishes this title text as an incomplete fragment ending after llamar. The official English original continues by saying that Neal Stephenson gives a label the name “dengo”; the missing Spanish ending has not been invented here.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I could
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Podría is a form of poder used for a possible or imagined option. Here the unspoken subject is yo, so it means “I could.” The same written form can also go with one other person or thing when context supplies that subject.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to restructure; reorganize
flow; order in which a program runs
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In computing, flujo can describe the path and order that program instructions follow. This is distinct from a stream of data.

example.es: El bucle cambia el flujo del programa.
example.en: The loop changes the program's flow.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: computer program
of the
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en cambio, “instead” or “on the other hand”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Learn en and cambio together. The expression contrasts the next choice or fact with what came before.

example.es: No fui en coche; en cambio, caminé.
example.en: I did not go by car; instead, I walked.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en cambio, “instead” or “on the other hand”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cambio alone often means “change.” With en, it forms a fixed connector that introduces a contrast or alternative.

example.es: No fui en coche; en cambio, caminé.
example.en: I did not go by car; instead, I walked.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to use
no separate English word; opens the dismissal que le den a…, “to hell with…”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In this fixed, forceful expression, que introduces a wished-for dismissal rather than a statement meaning “that.” Learn the whole expression together.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; part of que le den a…, “to hell with…”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Le is built into this colloquial dismissal and points toward the person or thing rejected after a. Natural English does not translate it separately.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate literal meaning here; supplies the force in que le den a…, “to hell with…”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Den is a special command-like form of dar, “to give.” In this idiom, translating dar literally would hide the real dismissive meaning.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces what is rejected in que le den a…
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the fixed dismissal que le den a…, a introduces the person or thing being rejected. With el it contracts to al.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: good (feminine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Buena is the feminine singular form of bueno. It is used before or after a feminine singular noun, such as práctica or decisión.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: practice; recommended way of doing something
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Práctica can mean repeated training, but in buena práctica it means a sound or recommended method used in a field.

example.es: Guardar copias es una buena práctica.
example.en: Keeping backups is a good practice.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to have; to have a certain quality about it
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In questions such as ¿qué tiene de especial?, tener asks what quality or feature something has. English often phrases the idea as “what is special about it?”

example.en: What is special about this place?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links tener to the quality being asked about
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In ¿qué tiene de bueno, malo o especial?, de connects tener to the quality under evaluation. Natural English usually uses “about it” instead of translating de alone.

example.en: What is special about this place?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: bad; wrong (masculine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Malo names the negative quality being evaluated. In ¿qué tiene de malo?, the complete question asks what is wrong or bad about something.

example.es: No veo nada malo en la idea.
example.en: I do not see anything wrong with the idea.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to compile (convert source code into an executable form)

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you introduce a contrasting fact or an alternative choice?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use en cambio: “instead,” “on the other hand,” or “by contrast.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: En cambio compares what follows with what was just mentioned. It can introduce an alternative action or show that two facts differ. A comma often follows it when it begins the new contrast.

example.es: Ana fue en tren; Luis, en cambio, condujo.
example.en: Ana went by train; Luis, on the other hand, drove.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you forcefully dismiss a person, thing, or idea in colloquial Spanish?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use que le den a…: “to hell with…” or “screw….”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is a strong, rude dismissal, so it is unsuitable for polite settings. After a, name what is being rejected. A plus el contracts to al: que le den al plan. The expression should not be translated word by word.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you ask what is bad, good, strange, or special about something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use ¿Qué tiene de…? followed by the word for the quality you are asking about.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tiene is the “it has” form of tener, but this question frame asks which quality something has. De connects tener to the quality word. Swap in especial, bueno, malo, raro, or another describing word. English usually reorganizes the question rather than matching each word in order.

example.en: What is special about this book?

cardDefinitions.promptEs: GOTO y el flujo de un programa
cardDefinitions.answerEn: GOTO jumps directly to a named point in code; overusing it can make a program's execution path hard to understand
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Structured programming normally uses functions, loops, and conditionals to keep control flow visible. A GOTO can be useful in limited cases, but arbitrary jumps can create tangled “spaghetti code” whose execution path is difficult to reason about.

regions.labelEs: QUE LE DEN A LA BUENA PRÁCTICA. ¿QUÉ PUEDE TENER DE MALO?

applications.exampleEs: QUE LE DEN A LA BUENA PRÁCTICA
applications.explanationEn: Que le den a supplies the fixed dismissal, and la buena práctica fills the slot naming its target.
Práctica is feminine singular, so buena uses its -a ending to match it.
Puede carries the possibility, and tener remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
The reusable evaluation frame is qué … tener de malo. Puede appears between qué and tener and is taught separately by the poder plus dictionary-form card.
